summary: Defines the SIP Replaces header, which logically replaces one existing SIP dialog with a new one. It is a building block for features such as attended transfer and call pickup in multi-party call control.

plainLanguage.summary: The Replaces header lets one phone call take the place of another. A caller sends a new INVITE that names the call it wants to replace, and the person receiving it swaps over to the new call and hangs up the old one. It is the building block for call transfer and for picking up a call on a different phone.

subtitle: A SIP header that lets one call take over from another, the building block behind attended transfer and call pickup.

tldr.problem: Features such as attended transfer or call pickup need one participant to be swapped for another in a conversation, and doing that with third-party call control needs a central controller that is not always wanted.
tldr.mechanism: A new INVITE carries a Replaces header holding the Call-ID, to-tag and from-tag of an existing dialog. The receiving user agent matches that dialog, accepts the new call and shuts the old one down.
tldr.outcome: Replacement works peer to peer, with proxies passing the header through untouched. Because it can disconnect people, the receiver must authenticate and authorize the requester before acting on it.

today: RFC 3891 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2004, and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it. It remains the definition of the SIP Replaces header.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
The Replaces header is a SIP extension header field, part of the SIP multiparty applications architecture framework. It is used to logically replace an existing SIP dialog with a new SIP dialog, which is especially useful in peer-to-peer call control environments.

One use is to replace one participant with another in a multimedia conversation. That functionality is already available through third-party call control, but the 3pcc model requires a central point of control, which may not be desirable. A method of performing the same call control primitives in a distributed, peer-to-peer fashion is therefore desirable.

Using a new INVITE with a new header for dialog matching was chosen over making implicit associations in an incoming INVITE based on call-id or other fields, because an INVITE already has the correct semantics for a new call, an explicit Replaces header makes the intent obvious, a unique call-id may be given to the replacement call which avoids dialog matching problems in the related user agents, and there are no adverse effects if the header is unsupported.

The header enables services such as attended call transfer, retrieve from park, and the transition from locally mixed conferences to two-party calls in a distributed peer-to-peer way. Although it is frequently used together with the REFER method, the two may be used independently.
sections.plainLanguage: The header names a call to be taken over by a new one. Using a brand new call to say so, rather than reusing the old one, keeps the intent obvious and avoids mixing up which call is which.

sections.title: Receiving a Replaces Header
sections.content:
The Replaces header contains the information used to match an existing SIP dialog: the call-id, the to-tag and the from-tag. On receiving an INVITE with a Replaces header, the user agent attempts to match this information with a confirmed or early dialog. The to-tag parameter is compared to the local tag and the from-tag parameter is compared to the remote tag.

If more than one Replaces header field is present in an INVITE, or if one is present in a request other than INVITE, the user agent server MUST reject the request with a 400 Bad Request response. The same response is required if another header field with contradictory semantics is present. If the header matches more than one dialog, the agent MUST act as if no match was found. If no match is found, the server rejects the INVITE and returns a 481 Call/Transaction Does Not Exist response, as it also does if the header matches a dialog that was not created with an INVITE. If the header matches a dialog that has already terminated, the agent SHOULD decline the request with a 603 Declined response, which prevents the irritating race in which the agent rings for a replacement call that is not wanted.

If the header matches an active dialog, the agent MUST verify that the initiator of the new INVITE is authorized to replace the matched dialog. If the initiator has been successfully authenticated as equivalent to the user being replaced, the replacement is authorized, for example when the two share the same Digest credentials or sign the replacement with S/MIME using the same private key. Alternatively the Referred-By mechanism can be used to show that the request was sent on behalf of the other participant in the matched dialog. Local policy may be applied on top.

If authorization succeeds, the agent attempts to accept the new INVITE, reassign the user interface and other resources of the matched dialog to the new INVITE, and shut down the replaced dialog. If it cannot accept the new INVITE, for example because it cannot establish the required quality of service or keying or because it has incompatible media, it MUST return an appropriate error response and MUST leave the matched dialog unchanged.

For a confirmed dialog, the agent checks for the early-only flag. If the flag is present it rejects the request with a 486 Busy response. Otherwise it accepts the new INVITE with a 200-class response and shuts down the replaced dialog with a BYE. If the header matches an early dialog that the agent itself initiated, it accepts the new INVITE with a 200-class response and shuts down the replaced dialog with a CANCEL. If it matches an early dialog that this agent did not initiate, it returns a 481 response and leaves the matched dialog unchanged.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiving side looks up the call named in the header. If it cannot find it, or finds it already finished, or finds more than one match, it turns the request down with a status code. If it finds the call, it checks that the requester is allowed to take it over before switching over.

sections.title: Sending a Replaces Header
sections.content:
A user agent that wishes to replace a single existing early or confirmed dialog with a new dialog of its own MAY send the target user agent an INVITE request containing a Replaces header field. The client places the call-id, to-tag and from-tag information for the target dialog in a single Replaces header field and sends the new INVITE to the target.

If the user agent only wishes to replace an early dialog, as in the call pickup example, the client MAY also include the early-only parameter. A client MUST NOT send an INVITE with a Replaces header field that attempts to replace an early dialog which was not originated by the target of the INVITE.

The mechanism does not provide a way to match multiple dialogs, nor a way to match an entire call, an entire transaction, or to follow a chain of proxy forking logic. For example, if Alice replaces Cathy in an early dialog with Bob but Bob does not answer, Alice's replacement request will not match other dialogs that Bob's user agent redirects to, nor other branches that its proxy forwards. Although the specification takes reasonable precautions against unexpected behaviour in the face of forking, implementations SHOULD only address replacement requests, that is set the Request-URI of the replacement request, to the SIP Contact URI of the target.
sections.plainLanguage: The sending side names exactly one call to be replaced and sends a new call to the same person. It must aim the new call straight at that person rather than let a proxy fan it out.

sections.title: Proxy Behaviour
sections.content:
Proxy servers do not require any new behaviour to support this extension. They simply pass the Replaces header field transparently as described in the SIP specification.

It is possible for a proxy, especially one that forks on application layer logic such as caller screening or time-of-day routing, to forward an INVITE request containing a Replaces header field to a completely orthogonal set of contacts other than the original request it was intended to replace. In that case the INVITE request with the Replaces header field will fail.
sections.plainLanguage: A proxy in the middle just forwards the header without reading it. If a proxy fans the call out to several places, the replacement simply fails, because the header names one call and one user.

sections.title: The Replaces Header
sections.content:
The Replaces header field indicates that a single dialog identified by the header field is to be shut down and logically replaced by the incoming INVITE in which it is contained. It is a request header only, and is defined only for INVITE requests. It MAY be encrypted as part of end-to-end encryption. Only a single Replaces header field value may be present in a SIP request.

The syntax uses the augmented Backus-Naur Form described in RFC 2234 and relies on a number of productions from RFC 3261. A Replaces header field MUST contain exactly one to-tag and exactly one from-tag, as they are required for unique dialog matching. For compatibility with dialogs initiated by RFC 2543 compliant user agents, a tag of zero matches both tags of zero and null. A Replaces header field MAY contain the early-flag.

The RFC prints three example header values: Replaces: 98732@sip.example.com;from-tag=r33th4x0r;to-tag=ff87ff, Replaces: 12adf2f34456gs5;to-tag=12345;from-tag=54321;early-only and Replaces: 87134@171.161.34.23;to-tag=24796;from-tag=0.
sections.plainLanguage: The header carries three things: which call it is, who answered it and who dialled it. The last two are called tags, and both are required so the right call is picked.

sections.title: The Replaces Option Tag
sections.content: The specification defines a new Require and Supported header option tag, replaces. User agents which support the Replaces header MUST include the replaces option tag in a Supported header field. User agents that want explicit failure notification if Replaces is not supported MAY include the replaces option in a Require header field. The RFC gives the example Require: replaces, 100rel.
sections.plainLanguage: An agent says it understands this header by listing it under Supported. A caller can insist on it with Require, so the call fails loudly rather than being ignored.

sections.title: Replacing an Early Dialog at the Originator
sections.content:
In this example Bob has just arrived in the lab and has not registered there yet. He hears his desk phone ring and quickly logs into a software user agent on a nearby computer. Among other things the software agent has access to the dialog state of his desk phone. When it notices that his phone is ringing, it offers him the choice of taking the call there. The software agent sends an INVITE with Replaces to Alice. When Alice's agent receives this new INVITE it cancels her original INVITE and connects Alice to Bob.

Bob's software agent adds the early-only flag, because the dialog it is replacing is still ringing rather than established. Alice answers the replacement with a 200 OK, cancels the original call to the desk phone, and the desk phone answers the cancel with a 200 OK and then reports 487 Request Terminated for the INVITE it never completed.
sections.plainLanguage: A man answers a ringing call on his laptop instead of the phone on his desk. The laptop takes over the call by naming the old one, and the desk phone gives up with a 487.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The extension specified in this document significantly changes the relative security of SIP devices. In SIP, even if an eavesdropper learns the call-id, To and From headers of a dialog, they cannot easily modify or destroy that dialog if Digest authentication or end-to-end message integrity are used.

This extension can be used to disconnect participants or replace participants in a multimedia conversation. Invitations with the Replaces header MUST only be accepted if the peer requesting the replacement has been properly authenticated using a standard SIP mechanism, Digest or S/MIME, and authorized to request a replacement of the target dialog. Implementations which support the Replaces header SHOULD also implement the Referred-By mechanism.

Deciding which requests are legitimately authorized to make dialog replacements is non-trivial and depends on a considerable amount of local policy configuration. In general there are four cases when an authorization for a replacement is reasonable: a replacement made by a party considered equivalent to the replaced party, a replacement made on behalf of the replaced party, a replacement made by a former participant, and a replacement made by a specifically authorized party.

The most common case is a replacement on the request of the replaced participant, which no longer wants to be involved, as in completing an attended transfer or converting a three-way call to a point-to-point call. Such replacements are typically triggered by a REFER request from the replaced participant, and the Referred-By mechanism identifies the apparent original requester. The example in the overview, where Alice replaces Bob, is a replacement by a former participant, and the RFC notes that this justification is more dangerous than the others. Implementations SHOULD NOT rely on this method as an authorization mechanism.

Since manipulating the dialog information could cause user agents to replace the wrong dialog, use of message integrity protection for that information is STRONGLY RECOMMENDED, and end-to-end encryption of it is also RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: This header can hang up other people's calls, so it must be authenticated. Being a former participant is not good enough on its own, because anyone who was ever on the call could then take it over.

messages.label: INVITE WITH REPLACES AND EARLY-ONLY
messages.note: Names the call to the desk phone by call-id, to-tag and from-tag.

viz.caption: THE ABNF FOR THE REPLACES HEADER AS PRINTED IN RFC 3891

data.title: Replaces
data.code:
Replaces        = "Replaces" HCOLON callid *(SEMI replaces-param)
replaces-param  = to-tag / from-tag / early-flag / generic-param
to-tag          = "to-tag" EQUAL token
from-tag        = "from-tag" EQUAL token
early-flag      = "early-only"

viz.caption: THE RESPONSES THE RFC REQUIRES FROM THE RECEIVING SIDE

items.label: BAD REQUEST
items.desc: More than one Replaces header, a Replaces header outside an INVITE, or a header with contradictory semantics.

items.label: CALL DOES NOT EXIST
items.desc: No dialog matched, more than one dialog matched, or the matched early dialog was not started by this agent.

items.label: DECLINED
items.desc: The matched dialog has already terminated.

items.label: BUSY
items.desc: The matched dialog is confirmed but the early-only flag was set.

items.label: ACCEPTED
items.desc: The new INVITE is accepted and the replaced dialog is shut down with a BYE or a CANCEL.
